content: Imagine living in a place where the sun is always shining, but the ground is dry and cracked. In Madho's village in Rajasthan, women have to walk for hours in the hot sand just to get a single pot of drinking water. Why do they value a single drop of water so much?
What would happen if the tap in your kitchen only gave one drop of water every second? How long do you think it would take to fill a single glass? Can you predict how many drops are in a spoonful?

content.title: Drop by Drop Fills the Bucket
content.description: Watch how a slow leak from a tap slowly fills up a large bucket over a few hours. Every drop counts!

content: This brings us to a very important concept. When a place does not have enough water for everyone's needs, we call it 'Water Scarcity'. To fight this, people collect and save rain using a method called 'Rainwater Harvesting'.

definition: A situation where there is a severe shortage of water for basic daily needs like drinking, washing, and farming.
The practice of collecting and storing rainwater, usually from rooftops, so it can be used later instead of letting it flow away.

question: Which of the following is the BEST way to save water at home?
options: Leaving the tap open while brushing teeth.
Using a bucket instead of a hose to wash your bicycle.
Ignoring a leaking tap because it is just a drop.

content: Many people think that a small leak from a tap doesn't waste much water. But a tap that drips once every second can waste over 10,000 liters of water in a year! That's enough to fill a small swimming pool.

Reflection: Close your eyes and imagine a day without any water. How would you brush your teeth, take a bath, or quench your thirst? What small changes can you make today to make sure water isn't wasted in your house?
Teachers, encourage students to calculate how many buckets of water their family uses daily. This practical math exercise builds deeper awareness of water consumption.

Connection: Saving water isn't a modern idea! Ancient Indians were experts at this. They built magnificent stepwells, called 'Baolis' or 'Vavs', hundreds of years ago to catch every single drop of rain during the monsoon, ensuring they had water all year round. The famous Rani Ki Vav in Gujarat is a great example!

Mastery Challenge: Become a Water Detective! Find one way to reuse water at home today. For example, collect the water used to wash vegetables and use it to water the plants in your garden or balcony. Keep a journal of how much water you saved!
